Green-Tao theorem is now formalized, in 25 hours, accepted by LeanEval!

I am experimenting with better ways to present an AI formalization project. I am pretty happy with this timeline movie! If anyone has any suggestions for how to improve the presentation of the process of the AI doing the formalization I would love to hear from you!
Just to be absolutely clear on this, are we using a version of lean where all the bugs mentioned in Leo's blog post are patched?

@Kevin Buzzard , no we are not.
It will take time for mathlib to adopt the new release, and then LeanEval can bump too.
E.g. this patch did not make it in the Aug 1 nightly mathlib release.
So are you worried about these claims, given that LLMs are perfectly capable of finding Leo's post?
I agree it's better to be sure, but just out of curiosity, have someone seen a real world example where telling the LLM "prove it for real, don't use a bug or something similar" is not enough?

I am not worried about these claims. These are specific bugs in specific metaprograms. The formalization of Green-Tao does not use those metaprograms. Since you are worried about it, here is the code. It does not use custom addDecl, inductDecl, mkProj, run_tac, CommandElabM, unsafeCast, meta/elab definitions, or partial/unsafe definitions.

I am not concerned about this particular bug. However, I am concerned about where else bugs may hide and be exploited! I guess Lean FRO will be doing a lot in this direction from now on.

Visualization wise, I would suggest having Claude use Verso to make these artifacts, the way lean-eval does already. Otherwise you might as well not put the lean snippets at all, as they are fairly hard to read. Presumably it shouldn't struggle too much.

Vasily Ilin said:

Since you are worried about it, here is the code.

Thanks. I thought that the philosophy was supposed to be that Challenge.lean only imports Mathlib. We are seeing more and more people posting Challenge.lean files which have other imports, and this is no exception. Can you tell your AI to never make a Challenge.lean file which imports anything other than Mathlib? Or have I got the philosophy wrong?

Ok so maybe I have the philosophy wrong. Thanks! @Kim Morrison I'm assuming then that you're happy with a defs file and a challenge file? My memory was that we wanted everything in one file.

Seems that you can get Green-Tao into around 100K lines of code.
If you have any auxiliary definition in the original file under LeanEval/, it looks like that the CI workflow is always going to produce a ChallengeDeps.lean file under generated/.

Seems that you can get Green-Tao into around 100K lines of code.

If you want to see more stats and the path that the AI took, take a look here.

Szemerédi's theorem is now proved and accepted by lean-eval.
It took 2.5 hours. 42,714 LOC total but only 275 lines had to be written from scratch, the other 41,702 are reused directly from the green-tao formalization. Below is the AI's own account of the timeline.

Timeline

07:41–08:29 — 48 min: scout Mathlib/Lean Pool/Tau Ceti/APAP, select the target, trace Green–Tao interfaces, extract the 90-file dependency closure, write 275 Lean lines plus 782 documentation lines, debug with Lean LSP, remove warnings, build, and measure memory.
08:29–08:40 — 10 min: commit/push and submission plumbing. The first private repository was inaccessible to the bot, so the exact commit had to be mirrored and resubmitted.
08:40–09:23 — 43 min: official evaluator. Its core comparison step alone took about 30 minutes; setup built comparator, Nanoda, sandbox tooling, and dependencies.
09:23–10:10 — 47 min: verify the recorded result, diagnose the leaderboard deployment’s GitHub 503, test permissions, file issue #58, notify the maintainer, and establish monitoring.

To me this is quite an interesting data point because when doing Green-Tao all I said to the AI about code quality was "Use reasonable defs, lemmas and file names and placement", and evidently that's enough for it to build a pretty reusable API.
